title: Learning plastering on August Bornhagen's jobs
summary: His stepfather took him on to learn the trade; he progressed from trowel to wall work and pay for carrying putty.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Did you get paid for that or just help?

Oh, yeah, he paid me. He gave me two dollars then. Oh, yeah. Yeah. He gave me two dollars. I don't think about no pay. I don't think about no pay, man. What a week. So, that evening when he finished, I'm coming home with him from work. It felt big. So, I came home. Mama said, well, you do all right? I said, yeah. He said, yeah. But it could. He said, but he's too small. I don't want to do that. I said, but he's going to school. Mama said, well, I'll tell you, Sam. I said, while he wants to, I'd like him to learn to trade. If he wants more schooling, he can work and go to night school. I said, but I managed for him to learn to trade. Especially while he wants to. He said, get bigger, he might not want to learn. So, he said, well, this is up to you. It's your son. I said, yes, yes, yes, yes. I want to learn to trade. So, he said, well, this is the last job. He says, I got for a while now. He says, Monday, I'm going to work for August Bornhagen. That was a white contract. Well, he had friends at Wake Forest Bornhagen. I was by the name of Arthur Adams. I was by the name of Louis Smoot. And, they had told him, Bornhagen had lots of work. He was idle. He was idle. He was idle. He was idle. He was idle. He sent him. So, he was idle. So, he was idle. So, he called Smoot up that Friday night and told me, you wind up on that Saturday and you go work for Bornhagen Monday. So, he said, I'm going work for Bornhagen. He says, and I don't know whether you want to take the apprentice. You know, the boss is not so anxious to take one of the apprentices. He says, well you can ask him anyway. He says, no, it doesn't. With regards to whether he gets paid or not, he says, I'm looking for him to get paid. He says, I want him to learn the trade. That's the principle part. So he says, all right, I'll talk to the old man about it. So he spoke to Barnagon about it. Barnagon says, Sam, I'm not going to talk to him. He says, I don't know. He says, in the first place, he said, his apprentices are sassy. In the next place, he said, they come to him about waste material and they want to pay for it. And my step says, this is my son. He said, I don't want to pay for it, I want to learn the trade. I just want to let him come on the job, learn the trade. I said, well, all right, Sam. He said, you can bring him, we'll try him out. So my stepdaddy brought me on the job. And I started the trade backwards. I started the fishing coach. They were doing the white coach job. They had the brownie then, they were doing the white coach job. So, my stepdad, there were two guys working the tops. And my stepdad was working the bottoms behind him. So, I stood in the back and my stepdad mixing the stuff. He had a old worn out trout. At that time, I was used to have greats, you know. But you know what a great is? A fireplace. And an iron frame around him and a great that hooks in it. It's a bird calling. And between the wood mantle and the great, there was a little section of plaster that went in there. So, I stepped at it. He had a piece of wood out there. He's a piece of cypress about 12 inches. I stepped at it, cut a piece off that, and he made me a hawk with the little handle and stuck a nail. And he gave me an old trout.
You actually, you did more than just carrying the stuff.
Well, I didn't carry that at that time. I was carrying because it wasn't for him, you know. He put me to carrying stuff right then.
He kept me around looking at it.

So, he gave me the, an old trout. And a little homemade hawk. And he said, alright, go play with that chimney now. He put some around that chimney. So, I went through around with the chimney. And what I got through with it, he called the other class and said, come see this. He was the first time the boy ever had a trowel in his hand. And the chimney was good. He didn't have to go over it.

So, the end of that week, he bought me a hawk. For all the fellas, when they get off in the evening, I wash their tools. And all of them would give me fifty cents. Alright. And you know what? Yeah, so, I got fifty cents from the other two classes.
And my stepdaddy gave me a dollar.

I give two dollars a week. So, One day, two dollars a week. Two dollars a week. Two dollars a week. Yeah. So, he let me go on working on those, those, those, those, the driver's chimney. They said, grace, you know. And my dream is I got to do them. Not much better, but faster. Yeah. So, then he start to have me put the rough, what we call rough end. It's the first white coat you put in, your rough coat. And he comes over with another level coat. And then he come over with what we call a skim coat. That hides all of what we call cat face. Any misses you catch it in the skim coats, you see. So, my stepdaddy bought me a horse. And he came over with a skim coat. And he came over with a skim coat. And he came over with a skim coat. And he started, started me into, what do you call roughing on, see. I'd go around there, roughing on the walls, and he'd come in behind me, you know. Level it out. And, uh, Bill, believe it or not, in about two months, I was making those bottoms with him. That's right. He'd make three walls to my one. And, uh, I was making those bottoms with him.
He'd make three walls to my one, but my wall was as good as his.
And I was 14 years old. That's right.

And, uh, then when I got into rough coats, I love to put the rough coat on, man. I was a demon. That was easy. Rough coats, yeah, it was easy. And, uh, so, uh, my step at him when I was white coating, he had his sinks because he was a bottom man, see. And, uh, I was doing half of the bottom with him. He'd be doing the bottom with the smoke,
waiting for them guys to get off the scalp, you know.
So, uh, smooth. I told my step at him, I said, why don't you get on the scalp with us? And try his hand on the ceilings. He says,

Try him on the ceilings. So, uh, I stepped at him, and she said, try him on the ceilings. So, uh, I stepped at him, and she said, I stepped at him, and she said, I was doing half of the bottom with him. And he was doing the bottom with the smoke, waiting for them guys to get off the scalp, you know. I said, I said, good wall, man. Try him on the ceilings. So, uh, I stepped at him, and he said, you want to get on the front of him on the ceilings? I said, yes, sir. I said, I'll jump on the scalp, and get my little corner. After a while, I got the hang of it. So, uh, I stepped at him, and, uh, he took a barn again, out in the trailer about three months, four months, and I was doing so much work. My step, I really told, uh, to him, he says, uh, he's going cap and cash. Cause he always had money on him, you know. He had money every night, he's going on the barn again. I said, Captain, he says, this boy had been here four months. I admit that's not a very long time. He said, he's working very good. I think he ought to get something. He said, well, Sam, he says, I don't be around here to see what the boy do. He said, I don't know. He's doing anything. Well, he wasn't. He just come in the morning, talk the men off. He might come around one o'clock. And you didn't see him in the motor lead knockoff times. So he said, but I tell you what, if you let him carry the putty for the white coat, I'll give him 75 cents a day. My daddy said, all right. When I got to carry the putty for the white coat, the same thing I cried to carry for him, I was carrying my buckets then. I was furnishing three men, putty, plaster and water, and still helping him on the bottles. And when, uh, when, uh, when, uh, in the rough coat and the scratch coat and the brownie, to take all the bathrooms, all the clothes closets. Most of those houses had clothes closets All the clothes closets. Most of those houses had a clothes closet. They had living room, two bedrooms, sometimes three bedrooms. All the bedrooms had a clothes closet. Kitchen had a broom closet. Bathroom had a linen closet.
